title: Fluid Dynamics Gets a Rewrite
hook: For two centuries physicists described fluids with essentially one theory. A modern idea — start from what symmetries a fluid breaks — has now rebuilt the definition from scratch.
key_points: From the 1800s to the early 2000s, one framework served for the behavior of fluids.
The new approach defines a fluid from the bottom up rather than patching the old equations.
The organizing principle is modern: identify the symmetries a system has and which ones it breaks.
Rebuilding from first principles extends the theory to regimes the classical version was never derived for.
content_html: The equations of fluid dynamics are old and astonishingly durable: written down in the nineteenth century, still used today to design aircraft wings and forecast weather. They were also derived the way nineteenth-century physics did things — by reasoning about a continuous substance and conserving the obvious quantities.
extra_html: Quanta's Charlie Wood reports on work that rebuilds the theory from the bottom up instead, using the organizing idea that has reshaped much of modern physics: symmetry. Ask what symmetries a system possesses and which ones it spontaneously breaks, and the equations that govern its long-wavelength behavior follow. Applied to fluids, that program reproduces the classical results but arrives at them as consequences rather than assumptions — and in doing so it clarifies what a fluid is, and extends the description to regimes the old derivation never covered.

related.title: What Is Pressure?
related.hook: Pressure is force spread over an area. Concentrate the same push on a tiny spot and it skyrockets — which is why a sharp knife cuts and a thumbtack pierces.

related.title: A 'Simple' Fluid That Cracks Like Glass
related.hook: Only springy, elastic fluids were thought able to fracture instead of just flowing. Then a Drexel University lab stretched an ordinary hydrocarbon liquid and heard it snap.

related.title: Turbulence, but every whirlpool is the same size
related.hook: Stir a superfluid and it can't swirl however it likes — circulation comes in fixed, indivisible units. That makes ultracold gases the cleanest lab for physics' oldest unsolved problem.

related.title: Surface Tension: Water's Stretchy Skin
related.hook: Water acts like it's wrapped in an invisible elastic skin — strong enough to let a bug walk across a pond and pull a droplet into a near-perfect sphere.

flashcards.prompt: Roughly how long did physicists rely on a single theory of fluids?
flashcards.back_html: About two centuries — from the 1800s to the early 2000s the same framework was used to understand fluid behavior.

flashcards.prompt: What is the modern insight driving the redefinition of fluids?

choices.text: Building the theory up from which symmetries a fluid has and breaks
Replacing continuous equations with computer simulation of every molecule
Treating every fluid as fundamentally quantum mechanical

flashcards.explanation_html: Rather than patching the classical equations, the new work defines a fluid from the bottom up using symmetry — the same organizing principle that reshaped particle physics.
